http://thepeninsulaqatar.com/article/16/.text: World / Europe Spanish jet downs drone in Romania after airspace breach Published: 16 Aug 2026 - 03:33 pm | Last Updated: 16 Aug 2026 - 03:43 pm AFP Bucharest: A Spanish fighter jet on Sunday shot down a drone that had breached Romanian airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova, national authorities and NATO said. A growing number of drones have crossed into NATO states in eastern Europe as Russia pursues its invasion of Ukraine. The interception of the drone -- which entered from Moldova -- was carried out by an F-18, deployed on NATO duties, at 5:01 am (0201 GMT), the Romanian defence ministry said in a statement. Debris fell in an unpopulated area of the Galati region, near the Ukrainian border, it added. Spain's defence ministry said on X that its air force had shown "its outstanding professionalism in the defence of European airspace". Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said he had spoken with his Romanian counterpart Oana Toiu, who thanked the pilots. NATO Air Command said on X that the mission involved two F-18s, which are part of a Spanish contingent of around 200 personnel and 11 aircraft based in Romania. Romania's eastern seaboard, bordering the Black Sea, is close to areas frequently targeted by Russian strikes. This was the fourth drone to be destroyed in the country since the start of Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022. And, in a separate incident on Sunday announced by the defence ministry, drone debris was found in the Black Sea, off Romania's city of Constanta. In July, Romania expelled a Russian embassy employee in what it called "a firm response" to drones repeatedly breaching the country's airspace. Romania shot down three drones on three consecutive days before the expulsion. Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border. Similar incidents have been reported elsewhere on NATO's eastern flank, including in Poland and the Baltic states. On Friday, NATO said Italian jets operating under the alliance's air-policing mission shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace. Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/Reuters France Fourteen men go on trial in Paris over deadliest small-boat Channel crossing Sinking of inflatable dinghy in 2021 resulted in 31 people dead or missing, including a seven-year-old child Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.07 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record. The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for. The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead also included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers. A team on a French fishing boat near British waters off Calais had raised the alarm when they saw several lifeless bodies floating in the water. According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes – between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England – began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea. Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived the tragedy. Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France . The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia. Among the defendants are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the ​smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched. Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators. The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as people who were seeking to make the journey themselves. However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain. For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by the French fishing vessel. A separate investigation is ongoing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel – who have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations. The UK’s Cranston inquiry , in its report released in February, found that systemic failings, missed opportunities and inadequate resourcing undermined the UK’s maritime search and rescue response on the night of the disaster. HM Coastguard was placed in an “intolerable position”, it said, with chronic staff shortages and limited operational capacity contributing directly to the failure to rescue people in the water. It found the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard. Families ​of some of the victims will travel from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said. “Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” the lawyers, Matthieu Chirez, Thomas Ricard and Camille Renouard, said in a statement. More on this topic Amid an escalating Russian sabotage campaign against Europe, Germany’s measured response to one recent attack is ringing alarm bells for many. But with rising populism at home and fears of escalation, it may be the best the country can offer. In early August, Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. Last week, Germany formally accused Russia of being behind the attempted attack, and in turn shuttered a Russian diplomatic mission, ramped up travel restrictions for Russian nationals, closed a Russian cultural center, and urged the EU to slap additional sanctions on Russia. Amid an escalating Russian sabotage campaign against Europe, Germany’s measured response to one recent attack is ringing alarm bells for many. But with rising populism at home and fears of escalation, it may be the best the country can offer. In early August, Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. Last week, Germany formally accused Russia of being behind the attempted attack, and in turn shuttered a Russian diplomatic mission, ramped up travel restrictions for Russian nationals, closed a Russian cultural center, and urged the EU to slap additional sanctions on Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin has denied involvement, accusing Berlin of planting evidence against Moscow. But Western officials have said the alleged attack is tied to a “broader pattern” of nefarious behavior from Moscow across Europe—involving drones, sabotage, cyberattacks, and disinformation campaigns—that is meant to sow discord and confusion among Ukraine’s allies. “This was an attack using military-grade material, carried out by Russian operatives on EU soil. And we will not tolerate it. We stand in full solidarity with Germany,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday . “Leipzig marks a new escalation on European soil, directly attributed to Russia. But it is part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents.” Instances of Russian sabotage and other forms of interference in Europe have risen sharply since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with some of the most dramatic attempted plots targeting Germany. These include the planned assassination of a major German arms CEO, the planned assassination of a German drone company CEO, and a plot to send mail bombs via a German parcel carrier. Germany’s response has appeared relatively muted. For instance, in the case of the reported Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the head of Germany’s largest arms company, Germany announced no specific punishments for Russia, and then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz made no direct comment. Many commentators have slammed Germany’s response to the attempted drone attack in Leipzig. “If every time Germany is attacked by Russia it does nothing[, then] Putin the bully will keep doing it,” wrote former British Defense Secretary Ben Wallace on X. “The German response so far reminds me of pre-2022,” Liana Fix, a senior fellow for Europe at the Council on Foreign Relations, told Foreign Policy . “It does not rise to the moment of Russian hybrid campaigns.” A more robust response from Germany might include seizing the ships that Russia uses to evade energy sanctions, as other countries are already doing, Fix said. Germany could also take action in the intelligence sphere, such as launching offensive cyberattacks—which would legally require sign-off by parliament. At least some of those efforts may be in the offing, Fix said, but could be difficult to trace due to their sensitive nature. Retired Lt. Gen. Doug Lute, who served as U.S. ambassador to NATO from 2013 to 2017, said many of the responses from Europe to Russia’s hybrid or gray-zone attacks have “been simply the most mild response, and that’s been to reveal them publicly, to disclose them, to bring them out into daylight.” It’s clear such responses have been “insufficient,” Lute said, but the “closing of diplomatic facilities by Berlin is a step in the right direction” and marks a “stronger” reaction than “most of the previous episodes.” Read More Wadephul and Dobrindt step onto a small elevated stage, where a lectern is set up. How Russia Could Escalate With progress in Ukraine grinding to a halt, Moscow could seek disruption off the battlefield. The AfD Is Now Germany’s Mainstream How the radical far-right party became the leader of the country’s opposition. Analysis | Paul Hockenos Meanwhile, any German response to Russia must factor in the rising power of far-right and -left parties, which have taken pro-Russian stances, as well as the plummeting popularity of Germany’s pro-Ukraine leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. In April, Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) polled at 28 percent, while Germany’s far-left party, Die Linke, polled at 11 percent. For comparison, Germany’s current chief of the ruling parliamentary coalition, the Christian Democratic Union, polled at 24 percent. The AfD also won its first state election last week, a major victory for the party. Many AfD and Die Linke voters do not see Russia as a threat. “Intelligence information and plausibility are not evidence,” wrote Die Linke parliamentarian Lea Reisner, in critique of the German government’s assertion that Russia was behind the attempted Leipzig Airport attack. “The current escalation is highly dangerous.” And despite broad support for Ukraine in Germany, many fear nuclear escalation , which Russia has proved willing to manipulate . “This nuclear angst is still there in Germany,” Fix said. Still, some Western officials view Germany openly accusing Russia of coordinating this attempted attack as a significant development in and of itself—particularly from the perspective of Baltic countries such as Estonia, which continue to face disruptive drone incursions tied to the Ukraine war. Germany was “very clear” in stating that there’s direct evidence that “Russia was behind this attack,” and it’s important that it was officially designated an “attack,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Foreign Policy . “This is the change I saw from the German side,” he said. There’s been a narrative that the “Baltics are next” and that it’s “somehow only our concern that Russia is provoking and organizing different attacks,” Tsahkna said, but it’s now “public for everybody in Europe that Russia is attacking Germany and attacking many other countries as well.” However, Tsahkna conceded that it’s “hard to say” what the “proportional” response should be, adding that it’s “clear that we are not going to organize” the same “kind of attacks” against Russia. The Baltics, which share land borders with Russia, have long expressed impatience over the broader Western response to the Kremlin’s hybrid attacks. The West “needed to respond already years ago,” Tsahkna said, emphasizing that Putin has been “turning on the heat” to test regional unity and NATO. “Putin is a master of playing with fears,” he added, and “the fear of escalation” is something he’s been using for years. One action Germany declined to take in response to the alleged attack was to invoke Article 4 of NATO’s founding treaty, which allows members to consult allies “whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened.” This is a rare step that’s only been taken nine times since NATO’s founding in 1949, but it does not immediately lead to further political or military responses. Yet Article 4 was invoked twice in September 2025 alone in response to Russian drones and fighter jets violating the airspace of Poland and Estonia. In late September 2025, after the Article 4 consultations, NATO warned Russia it would employ “all necessary military and non-military tools to defend ourselves and deter all threats from all directions.” That same month, U.S. President Donald Trump said NATO countries should shoot down unauthorized Russian aircraft that enter their airspace. But even after such steps and warnings, Russia continues to be linked to an escalating series of provocative incidents across Europe. Between its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and February 2026, Russia conducted 151 hostile operations in Europe, according to a report by the Netherlands-based International Centre for Counter-Terrorism released earlier this year. Between August 2024 and February 2026 there were 144 reported drone sightings over a dozen European states, according to a July report from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies. The report concluded that “it is highly likely that the Kremlin conducted a UAV campaign over Europe.” As the problem metastasizes, European leaders are also struggling with precisely what to call it. Germany has said it’s not at war with Russia but the target of “hybrid warfare.” The situation has sparked debate over whether such terminology falls short in terms of describing the issue and has contributed to a lackluster response. There’s a growing push for Russia’s actions to be labeled as state-sanctioned terrorism. “We need to name it as it is, and state-supported terrorism is a very precise thing, and we know how to act and how we deal with other terrorist acts,” Tsahkna said. “Putin understands only the clear messages and actions.” EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas last week also said the failed attack “has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” while conceding that there’s still an open question about what to do about it. The use of the word “terrorism” by NATO allies marks an “interesting escalation,” said Lute, noting that the only time Article 5 was ever invoked came after the 9/11 terror attacks on the United States. But in terms of defining the problem, Lute said it’s especially important for NATO to stop treating Russian hybrid attacks on a “one-off” basis and “compile the record.” “There’s power in accumulating them and assembling them into a package so that you can see the breadth and depth and the persistence of the attacks,” Lute said, adding that there could also be more steps taken at NATO headquarters, ranging from table-top exercises to consultations with key allies, to send a signal to the Kremlin that the alliance is not sitting on its hands. “We’ve progressed far enough along this spectrum towards armed conflict, towards armed attack, that NATO has got to be seen as more active and not passive,” Lute said. “People say these kinds of political responses are not important because Putin is continuing,” Tsahkna said, but the Russian president “is very carefully watching what we do, how united we are.” This post appeared in FP's The Reading List newsletter. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA Northern Ireland Drumcree talks break up without agreement on fifth day of standoff Dispute over march will go to legal appeal on Monday after talks hosted by Northern Ireland secretary end Lisa O’Carroll Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.16 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. Speaking on Thursday night after the latest talks with the Orange Order and residents of Garvaghy Road broke up, Bryant said: “I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven’t come to a settled agreement, and it’s a shame, but my door remains open.” Last Friday’s Parades Commission decision to grant the Orange Order the right to hold a procession down the nationalist Garvaghy Road plunged Northern Ireland into one of its most perilous periods since the 1998 peace deal. A legal appeal by the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition originally scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Monday to facilitate any further talks. “Obviously we’ll have to see how that plays out,” Bryant said, indicating he would not be intervening unilaterally. “I would say that the law, in the end, is the law.” Five days of talks ended in deadlock, he said, outlining the compromises on the table for the first time. “We’ve discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn’t exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we’ve not managed to come to agreement on any of all that.” View image in fullscreen Chris Bryant arrives at Hillsborough castle for talks on Thursday. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA Earlier in the week, reports suggested one option was a “one and done” parade involving just a dozen people without insignia in October. This would have been on condition the Orange Order would never apply for permit for that parade route again. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said “the reality is” there was “no such thing as half a march”. “There’s a march or there’s not a march – simply that,” he said. Jamie Bryson, a legal adviser to the Orange Order, who earlier this week said he would “not surrender” said he would accept Monday’s ruling. “The challenge that we would put down to the Garvaghy Road residents – they’re going to the court of appeal on Monday – if the court of appeal upholds this determination, commit to accepting the law and walk away, and we’ll do the same,” he said. “Abide by the law, and if the court of appeal upholds the determination, get off the road, stop breaking the law and allow the parade to go ahead. If we lose, we’ll accept that.” Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant Read more The dispute began last week after the march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998 , a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness” and by the taoiseach as “incomprehensible and wrong”. The dispute, which threatened to collapse Stormont and has returned Northern Ireland to bleak days of the past, has also revived the interest of key US Democrats. Richie Neal, the US representative for Massachussetts’ 1st congressional district, described the parade as “needlessly provocative”. The Congressional Friends of Ireland Caucus, which Neal sits on, wrote to Bryant urging him to use his powers to reverse the Parades Commission decision. “Over the last three decades, the progress made on the island of Ireland has been nothing short of extraordinary. Twenty-eight years have passed since the signing of the Good Friday agreement, and a generation has grown without a single memory of the Troubles,” the lawmakers wrote. “Without decisive action, we risk reopening one of the most painful chapters of Northern Ireland’s history and undermining nearly three decades of peace, stability and reconciliation made possible by the Good Friday agreement.” The Northern Ireland Policing Board has been told that the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) operation around the parading dispute has topped £3m.
